title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

content.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder, representing the preorder and inorder traversal of the same binary tree (with unique values), construct and return the original binary tree.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","preorder array, inorder array"],["Output","The root of the reconstructed original binary tree"],["Key Insight","preorder's first remaining value is always the current subtree's root; its position in inorder splits left from right"],["Constraints","Up to 3000 nodes, unique values"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Reconstruct a tree from two traversal orders\"","Preorder always visits the root FIRST, so its front value identifies the root; inorder places all left-subtree values before the root and all right-subtree values after it, giving a clean recursive split"]]}

blocks.text: In a preorder traversal, the very first value of any subtree's segment is always that subtree's root. Looking up that same root value's position within the corresponding inorder segment tells us exactly how many values belong to the left subtree (everything before it) and how many belong to the right subtree (everything after it), letting the same idea be applied recursively to build both children.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reconstructing an Org Chart From Two Different Meeting Sign-In Orders
blocks.text: Picture reconstructing a company's reporting hierarchy from two clues: one list always names the boss of a group FIRST before its members (preorder), and another list always lists a group's members with the boss appearing exactly in the middle, sorted by team (inorder). Combining these two clues, level by level, rebuilds the exact hierarchy.

blocks.caption: preorder's front value is the root; its position in inorder splits left subtree from right subtree

blocks.text: Reconstructed preorder check: 3 9 null null 20 15 null null 7 null null (matches the input preorder as expected, confirming the tree shape: root 3, left child 9, right subtree rooted at 20 with children 15 and 7).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The very first value remaining in the preorder array (processed left to right, consumed one at a time) is always the CURRENT subtree's root.

Observation 2: Finding that root value's position within the CURRENT inorder segment splits it into two parts: everything before the root belongs to the left subtree, everything after belongs to the right subtree.

Observation 3: Recursively applying this exact idea to the left inorder segment (consuming the next preorder values for it) builds the left subtree, and then the same for the right inorder segment builds the right subtree.

Observation 4: Repeatedly searching the inorder array LINEARLY for each root's position is wasteful; precomputing a hash map from value to its inorder index, ONCE upfront, turns each lookup into O(1).
This leads to a recursive construction using a shared preorder pointer (always consuming the next value as the current root) and a precomputed inorder value-to-index map for O(1) split-point lookups.
Recursively construct the tree the same way, but LINEARLY search the inorder array for the current root's position on every single recursive call, instead of using a precomputed map.

codes.python:
def build_tree_brute(preorder, inorder):
    if not preorder or not inorder:
        return None
    root_val = preorder[0]
    root = TreeNode(root_val)
    mid = inorder.index(root_val)                      # LINEAR search every single call
    root.left = build_tree_brute(preorder[1:mid + 1], inorder[:mid])
    root.right = build_tree_brute(preorder[mid + 1:], inorder[mid + 1:])
    return root

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Searching inorder directly for each root implements the core idea straightforwardly.
This costs O(n) per search (and per array slice), compounding to O(n squared) overall; a precomputed hash map turns each lookup into O(1).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case, due to repeated linear searches and array slicing.
Space: O(n squared) worst case for the sliced sub-arrays created at every call.
Limitation: a precomputed value-to-index map, combined with index-based ranges instead of actual array slicing, brings this down to O(n) overall.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Precompute a hash map from each inorder value to its index, ONCE upfront (values are guaranteed unique). Maintain a single shared pointer into preorder, always consuming its NEXT value as the current subtree's root. Use the precomputed map to find that root's index within the inorder array in O(1), splitting the CURRENT inorder range (tracked via index bounds, not actual slicing) into a left range and a right range. Recursively build the left subtree using the left range (consuming preorder values as needed), then the right subtree using the right range.
Use a precomputed value-to-index map for O(1) split lookups, and index-range bounds (not array slicing) to avoid unnecessary copying.

codes.python:
def build_tree(preorder, inorder):
    idx_map = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(inorder)}      # value to index, built ONCE
    pre_idx = [0]
    def build(in_left, in_right):
        if in_left > in_right:
            return None
        root_val = preorder[pre_idx[0]]
        pre_idx[0] += 1                                          # consume the NEXT preorder value
        node = TreeNode(root_val)
        mid = idx_map[root_val]                                    # O(1) lookup
        node.left = build(in_left, mid - 1)                          # left range
        node.right = build(mid + 1, in_right)                          # right range
        return node
    return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

blocks.text: Since preorder always visits a subtree's root before any of its descendants, consuming preorder values strictly left to right correctly assigns each value to its proper subtree's root in the right order; the precomputed inorder index map correctly and instantly identifies how many values belong to the left versus right subtree at every step, without ever needing to search or physically copy sub-arrays.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each node processed once with O(1) map lookups.
Space: O(n) for the map, O(h) recursion depth.

blocks.text: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal rewards recognizing the roles of the two traversal orders precisely: preorder identifies roots in order, inorder identifies the left/right split for each root.

items: Slicing arrays at every recursive call (creating new copies) instead of tracking index ranges into the original arrays, causing unnecessary overhead.
Forgetting to advance the shared preorder pointer in the correct order (root must be consumed before recursing into children).

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "preorder gives roots in order, inorder gives the left-right split for each root" demonstrates the core algorithmic insight immediately.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "reconstruct a tree from preorder and inorder traversals", think: preorder's front value is the root, its inorder position splits left from right.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The naive linear-search-plus-slicing approach costs O(n squared) worst case; the precomputed-map, index-range approach costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: a precomputed value-to-index map combined with index-range recursion (avoiding array slicing).
Core Idea: preorder's front value is always the current subtree's root; its position in inorder splits left subtree values from right subtree values.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for the naive approach, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n squared) worst case for the naive approach's copies, O(n) for the optimized approach's map.
Most Important Observation: a precomputed map turns repeated linear searches into O(1) lookups.
Interview Difficulty: a classic medium-level tree reconstruction problem.
One line memory trick: preorder gives the root, inorder gives the split.
